title: Lichens

paragraphs.text: Lichens grow equally well on high mountains and on river stones, on walls of old houses and the bark of trees, even on glass and old cars. There are more than 18,000 known species in the world (and researchers suggest there may be as many as 24,000), yet there is just one common word to describe this incredible diversity of life. Lichens are one of the planet’s most successful colonisers, and are unlike other forms of life on Earth. They are not plants but are composite structures, meaning they consist of different organisms: fungi and a partner – usually a type of algae. The partnership is stable and resilient, and makes it possible for lichens to flourish in environments we think of as hostile.

By suspending their metabolic system, lichens are able to tolerate periods of severe heat and drought, even radiation, that would kill most other life forms. An experiment was conducted by the European Space Agency in 2005, when two species of lichens were sealed in a capsule and launched into space. Once in orbit, the capsules were opened and the lichens were exposed to the vacuum of space, its near-absolute zero temperature, and ultraviolet rays. After 15 days the lichens were brought back to Earth. Both species were found to be in perfect health, with no discernible damage from their time in orbit.

While lichens dry rather easily, they wet quickly too. When moisture and sunlight occur together, they will start to photosynthesise within minutes. But the window of opportunity for photosynthesis is as little as an hour or two a day before they run out of moisture. By contrast, trees, with vast reserves of water, can photosynthesise and grow all hours. It is no surprise, then, that lichens are perhaps the slowest growing of all known organisms. However, it would be a mistake to think of lichens as harmless. When they are looked at with enough magnification, it is clear that lichens aggressively defend their habitat. They deter invasions of their living space by other lichens with specifically made poisons.

Lichens have been part of human culture for many centuries. Long-beard lichen is often seen growing in the wild as long, fluffy strands through the branches of trees. In the past it was used as a decoration for Christmas trees in various parts of the world, although today a synthetic substitute is used. Lichens are still used in the perfume industry, and around the Mediterranean alone some 8,000 tonnes are harvested every year. It is not that lichens have a pleasant scent of their own, but the oil extracted from a blend of lichens can be used as a fixative that easily takes Turn over ▶ on other scents, then slowly releases them. Some ancient cultures used lichens to make products like babies’ nappies, knowing what modern science is now proving: that the acid present in lichens has qualities that prevent skin irritations and rashes.

One researcher of lichens is the New Zealander David Galloway, who has an unusual scientific laboratory – the cemetery near his home. It is a place of great stability and lichens do not like change, according to Galloway. He has calculated that the lichen species Rhizocarpon geographicum grows between 2 and 20mm per century. This sort of information has proved useful out in the field. For example, the size of lichens growing on a piece of rock in the mountains can tell Galloway the maximum length of time the rock has been in that location. This dating technique has allowed him to determine the retreat rate of glaciers, an important issue for scientists studying climate change.

Another practical application stems from the fact that lichens have no roots. As a result, they must take all their nutrition from the rain and air. This means that the health of lichens can give a first indication that pollution may be developing, without relying on expensive instruments. Some years ago, Galloway successfully used a lichen survey for this purpose at a factory near the city of New Plymouth.

Another favourite location for Galloway is Rangitoto Island, which was created around 700 years ago by a volcanic eruption. The lava fields of Rangitoto are an ideal habitat for lichens, and the island is a perfect place to study the history of plant settlement. Galloway’s research has revealed that the spores of lichens arrived, carried on the wind, and anchored themselves on the island. For centuries the rocks would not have looked much different. But spreading slowly, growing, dying and decomposing, the lichens built what was necessary for life – the first thin layer of soil. Into it, airborne dust and guano from seabirds added nutrients and, with time, more complex lichens arrived, then ferns, shrubs and bushes. The lichens then stabilised the environment by binding stones and organic matter together, preventing erosion by the weather, and so protecting the other life forms taking hold on the island.
